title: Boss: the checkout API that stalls at lunchtime
summary: From counters and stacks to three fixes: an async price client, a concurrent cache warm-up, and a refresh loop that never blocks a pool thread.

steps.title: The ticket
body: **INC-4471: checkout p99 at 9 s between 12:00 and 13:00, CPU 20%.**
$ dotnet-stack report -n Checkout | grep -A1 GetResultCore | grep Checkout! | sort | uniq -c
Three places block pool threads on tasks. Fix all three. Each check holds the fake dependency's answer until the test says so, so
blocking code cannot pass by luck.

steps.title: 1. The price client
prompt: Replace `decimal GetPrice(string sku)` with **`Task<decimal> GetPriceAsync(string sku, CancellationToken ct)`** on `PriceClient`.
- Await `api.GetCentsAsync(sku, ct)`, and pass the **same token** on, so an aborted request also stops the call.
- Return the price in currency units: cents / 100 as a `decimal` (1999 cents is `19.99m`).
solution: public async Task<decimal> GetPriceAsync(string sku, CancellationToken ct)
template: Dojo.Check("GetPriceAsync returns while the price service is working", !dojoTask.IsCompleted,
"It only returned after the price service answered: something blocks the thread.");
Dojo.Check("The request's token is passed on to the price service", dojoApi.LastToken == dojoCts.Token,
"Pass ct to api.GetCentsAsync(sku, ct): when the caller gives up, the call to the price service should stop too.");
public Task<int> GetCentsAsync(string sku, CancellationToken ct) { LastToken = ct; return _answer.Task; }

forbid.message: Does not block on the task

hints: Make the method `async Task<decimal>`, take a `CancellationToken ct`, and `await api.GetCentsAsync(sku, ct)`.
`public async Task<decimal> GetPriceAsync(string sku, CancellationToken ct) { var cents = await api.GetCentsAsync(sku, ct); return cents / 100m; }`

steps.title: 2. The cache warmer
prompt: At startup (and, it turns out, on the first request of every new pod) `Warm` loads the product counts of three regions,
`"eu"`, `"us"` and `"ap"`, one after the other, blocking each time with `Task.Run(...).Result`.
Write **`static async Task<int> WarmAsync(Regions regions)`** that loads all three **at the same time** with
`regions.LoadAsync(name)` (a `Task<int>`) and returns the sum. The fake only answers once all three loads are in flight.
template: Dojo.Check("WarmAsync returns while the regions are loading", !dojoTask.IsCompleted, "It only returned after the loads finished: something blocks.");
Dojo.Check("All three regions load at the same time", dojoDone == dojoTask && dojoRegions.AllAtOnce,
"The fake answers only when all three loads are in flight. Start all three, then await Task.WhenAll.");
Dojo.Eq("The regions were eu, us and ap", "ap,eu,us", string.Join(",", dojoRegions.Names.Order()));
if (dojoDone == dojoTask) Dojo.Eq("WarmAsync returns 10 + 20 + 30", 60, await dojoTask);

forbid.message: Does not block on a task

hints: Start the three loads first (a `Select` or three variables), then `await Task.WhenAll(...)`, which gives you an `int[]`.
`var counts = await Task.WhenAll(names.Select(n => regions.LoadAsync(n))); return counts.Sum();`

steps.title: 3. The rates refresher
prompt: `RatesRefresher` refreshes exchange rates every few seconds with a `System.Threading.Timer` whose callback does
`refresh(ct).Wait()`: a blocked pool thread on every tick, and one exception kills it silently.
Write **`static async Task RunRefreshLoopAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task> refresh, TimeSpan every, CancellationToken ct)`**:
- use a **`PeriodicTimer`** (`await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct)`) and call `await refresh(ct)` on every tick;
- if a refresh throws, print `refresh failed: {message}` and **keep going**;
- when `ct` is cancelled, **return quietly** (no exception out of the method).
The tests use a 10 ms period: the second refresh throws, the third cancels the token.
starter: static async Task RunRefreshLoopAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task> refresh, TimeSpan every, CancellationToken ct)
solution: static async Task RunRefreshLoopAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task> refresh, TimeSpan every, CancellationToken ct)
template: if (n == 2) throw new InvalidOperationException("rates service down");
var dojoFinished = await Task.WhenAny(dojoLoop, Task.Delay(3000)) == dojoLoop;
if (dojoFinished) { try { await dojoLoop; } catch (Exception e) { dojoError = e; } }
Dojo.Check("The loop stops once the token is cancelled", dojoFinished, "It was still running 3 seconds after cancellation.");
Dojo.Check("Cancellation ends the loop quietly", dojoFinished && dojoError is null, "It threw " + dojoError?.GetType().Name + ": catch OperationCanceledException when ct is cancelled.");
Dojo.Eq("Exactly three refreshes ran (it kept going after the failure)", 3, dojoCalls);
Dojo.Check("The failure was reported", dojoOut.ToString().Contains("refresh failed: rates service down"), "Print: refresh failed: {e.Message}");
hints: `using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(every); while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct)) { ... }` and put `await refresh(ct)` in a try/catch inside the loop.
`WaitForNextTickAsync(ct)` throws `OperationCanceledException` when `ct` is cancelled: wrap the whole loop in `try { ... } catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested) { }`.
explain: `PeriodicTimer` (.NET 6+) never overlaps ticks: if a refresh takes longer than the period, the next tick waits. A `System.Threading.Timer`
callback fires on schedule even while the last one is still running, which is how a slow dependency turns into a pile of blocked threads.
The `when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)` filter matters: a timeout *inside* `refresh` also throws `OperationCanceledException`, and that
one is a failure to report, not a shutdown.
